question.prompt:
Problems \(8,\) \(9,\) and \(10\) use the data found in the accompanying paragraph and figures.

Bake Sale

Four friends, Art, Roger, Paul and Trisha, bake cookies, and all cookies have the same thickness. The shapes of the cookies differ, as shown.

• Art’s cookies are trapezoids:

[Figure 1](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig1.svg)

• Roger’s cookies are rectangles:

[Figure 2](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig2.svg)

• Paul’s cookies are parallelograms:

[Figure 3](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig3.svg)

• Trisha’s cookies are triangles:

[Figure 4](figures/2003_AMC_8_Q08_question_fig4.svg)

Each friend uses the same amount of dough, and Art makes exactly \(12\) cookies.

How many cookies will be in one batch of Trisha’s cookies?

solutions.explanation:
Because all cookies have the same thickness, their dough amounts are proportional to their areas. Thus we can compare Art’s and Trisha’s cookies using the marked dimensions.

Art’s trapezoid has parallel bases of \(3\) and \(5\) inches and perpendicular height \(3\) inches. Its area is
\[
\frac{(3+5)\cdot3}{2}=12\text{ square inches}.
\]
Trisha’s triangle has perpendicular base and height of \(3\) and \(4\) inches, so its area is
\[
\frac{3\cdot4}{2}=6\text{ square inches}.
\]
Each Trisha cookie therefore uses half as much dough as an Art cookie. The dough for each Art cookie makes two Trisha cookies, so Trisha’s batch contains \(12\cdot2=\boxed{24}\) cookies, choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
solutions.title: Compare the cookie areas
